newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's exports seen rising modestly.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's exports seen rising modestly.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil domestic exports for February are likely to show a modest rise, but the manufacturing sector continues its struggle to make headway in a tough market, economists said on Tuesday.
A Reuter poll of 16 financial institutions this week showed an average forecast of 1.5 percent rise year-on-year in nominal terms for non-oil exports in February.

Opinions varied widely, ranging from a five percent fall to a 10 percent rise. The forecasts were partly influenced by recent industrial output data and reinforced perceptions that export growth would continue to be weak, economists said.

"The wide range of forecasts partly reflects some uncertainty on manufacturing performance following the release of industrial output, which was weaker than expected," said Kaan Quan Hon, DBS Securities director of economic research.
Singapore's industrial production fell 7.2 percent in January against the same month of 1996, prompting some analysts to trim forecasts for gross domestic product (GDP).

Industrial output was dragged lower by electronics, down a sharp 10.9 percent in January. And electronics are a sizeable component of Singapore's exports, accounting for 58 percent of total exports in 1996.
Economists said recent U.S. orders for semi-conductors and computer parts would boost domestic manufacturing in the mid-term.
But Singapore's electronics and manufacturing sectors would start posting positive gains only in the second half of the year, they said.
"There's uncertainty about first-half growth. Manufacturing is consolidating but it could be a long haul before we're out of the woods," economist with H.G. Asia Song Seng Wun said.
He said manufacturing as a whole was still problematic.
Semi-conductor producers were still suffering weak prices and excess capacity, while some consumer electronic firms facing stiff competition from the region were shrinking.
But economists were mostly encouraged by improved U.S. book-to-bill ratios for semi-conductors, a barometer of orders for primary producers.
The range of forecasts was attributed largely to disagreement over just when the recovery would take place, and which months in the first half of the year would be most volatile.

Some economists cautioned, however, that February non-oil exports were prone to volatility anyway, being caught in the middle of two major holidays this year -- Chinese New Year and the end of Ramadam, the Moslem month of fasting.
"Exporters tend to do a lot of front-loading in December and January to make up for fewer days in February," Song said.
Some companies close for as long as 10 days to celebrate the Chinese New Year.
Others economists said a lower base in February 1996, at Singapore $5.9 billion compared with an average $7.7 billion for the three months preceding it, also influenced the disparate range.
Some economists had predicted total volumes in February could rise as much as 10 percent to $6.6 billion.
